newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Moslem women prevented from visiting grave.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Moslem women prevented from visiting grave.

text.p: Distraught Bosnian Moslem women from Srebrenica trying to mourn the massacre of their menfolk had to cancel plans to visit a grave site in Serb-held territory on Friday.

Fearing a possible violent clash with an angry Serb mob, U.S. and Russian peacekeeping troops prevented the convoy of some 100 Moslem women from crossing into Serb-controlled territory at a road checkpoint.

International police monitors advised the Srebrenica women that the visit was too risky, especially a day after NATO launched a raid against two Serbs indicted for war crimes, U.N. spokesman Andrea Angelli said.
"We are recommending that you do not go," an international policeman told the women as U.S. helicopters flew overhead.
"I can only advise that it is very dangerous there now."
The Srebrenica women had applied months ago for permission to visit one of the mass grave sites where their loved ones are believed buried.
After pleading with the peacekeeping troops for four hours, the Moslem women visited another grave site in Nezuk, in Moslem-Croat federation territory .
"I would like to at least find their bones, and to know where my children were buried," said 64-year old Dzemila Delalic.
Bosnian Serb television showed footage of an angry crowd of Serbs near Sapna who vowed to halt any attempt by Moslems to visit Serb-controlled territory.
The television referred to "alleged mass graves".
Two U.N. cars were stoned in the area on Friday by Serbs who apparently suspected the vehicles were carrying Moslems, Angelli said.

In July 1995, thousands of unarmed Moslem men from Srebrenica were executed or ambushed as they fled conquering Bosnian Serb forces. Human rights workers say it was Europe's worst atrocity since World War Two.

Bosnian Serb army commander General Ratko Mladic and former ex-president Radovan Karadzic have been indicted by the U.N. war crimes tribunal for orchestrating the slaughter of the Srebrenica men but the two remain at large.
A NATO raid this week on two suspects linked to ethnic expulsions of Moslems and Croats in the Prijedor region raised expectations that Mladic or Karadzic might be arrested soon.

Only a small number of the bodies of Srebrenica victims have been recovered since a peace agreement was signed in December 1995. Investigators suspect that many bodies were dumped in the nearby Drina river.
